chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fazalat ibn Ayyub, from Aban, from Zurara, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about the man who prays in Mecca, placing the Maqam (Station of Ibrahim) behind his back while he is facing the Qiblah. He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no harm. He may pray wherever he wishes in the Masjid, either in front of the Maqam or behind it. The most superior of these spots is Al-Hateem, and Al-Hijr, and by the Maqam. And Al-Hateem is parallel to the Door (of the Ka'bah).'

key_terms.الْحَطِيمُ: Al-Hateem, the semi-circular wall area adjacent to the Ka'bah
key_terms.الْحِجْرُ: Al-Hijr, the area enclosed by the semi-circular wall
key_terms.الْقِبْلَةِ: The Qiblah, the direction of prayer towards the Ka'bah
key_terms.الْمَقَامَ: The Station of Ibrahim (AS) in the Ka'bah

ai.seo_question: What is the most superior spot for prayer in the Masjid al-Haram according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the flexibility of prayer orientation within the Masjid al-Haram, affirming that placing the Maqam Ibrahim behind the back is permissible while identifying Al-Hateem and Al-Hijr as the most virtuous spots. It reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the sanctity of specific architectural features within the Kaaba complex, linking physical proximity to spiritual merit. The ruling underscores the principle that in the Sacred Mosque, the entire space is considered a place of worship, allowing for varied orientations relative to the Maqam.
